assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and realised in strontium and other species, brought fractional frequency uncertainty to the 1e-18 level. This is a measurement advance in the strict sense: it improves the best instrument for time by two orders of magnitude over the caesium standard and enables relativistic geodesy, tests of constancy of constants, dark-matter searches and a redefinition of the second. It opens new ways of observing nature, which is the criterion I weight most.
assessment.attribution: Katori made the magic-wavelength lattice idea and first demonstrated it; Ye's group carried the technique to record accuracy and stability with spin-polarised fermions, cavity-stabilised lasers and comb transfer. Two laureates fit cleanly. Other contributors (e.g. ion-clock work already recognised in 2012, Hall and Hansch for combs in 2005) are not credited here, so the pair is defensible.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, others) confirm 1e-18 level performance, with comparisons between clocks. The interpretation is stable and the field is active. Recognition is timely and arguably approaching overdue.
uncertainties: Competition with trapped-ion optical clocks, whose pioneers were partly recognised in 2012, could be raised as a credit-sharing concern.
The formal SI redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the final practical impact is still in progress.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres gave a room-temperature solid-state qubit and a nanoscale sensor for magnetic field, electric field, temperature and strain, with applications from condensed matter to biology. It rests on clear single-spin experimental demonstrations and has clearly spawned many follow-on techniques and a whole sensing field, which fits my attention to measurement methods and to impact beyond physics.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko made the first optical detection of single NV spins and the coherent control; Lukin's group drove the sensing and quantum-register developments. Other groups (Awschalom, Hanson, Yacoby, Walsworth, Budker) contributed substantially, so the three-person selection leaves out important contributors, but a fair configuration exists.
assessment.maturity: Replicated by many groups worldwide for two decades; commercial devices exist. Mature, with an unresolved question of how to divide credit between single-spin control and sensing.
uncertainties: Credit between the basic demonstration, quantum registers and sensing is spread across more than three people.
Overlap with B008 means the committee would have to avoid double counting spin-photon interface work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter waves into inertial and gravitational sensors, with absolute gravimeters, gyroscopes, measurements of G and the fine-structure constant, and equivalence-principle tests. It is a clear case of a new measurement principle, directly relevant to precision measurement and to practical gravimetry, and with large fundamental physics reach.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's theory of the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer, Pritchard's first atom interferometer with gratings and Kasevich and Chu's light-pulse interferometer are the key steps. Chu's absence from the credited names is notable (he already shared the 1997 prize for laser cooling), and Schmiedmayer's contributions are left to a fourth slot. A three-person split is feasible but contestable.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed in many labs, with commercial and field-deployed instruments. The most exciting uses (gravitational-wave detection, dark-matter searches) are not yet realised, but the core invention is mature.
uncertainties: Uncertain how the committee would weigh the overlap with the earlier laser-cooling prize and Chu's role.
Priority disputes among the early interferometer demonstrations of 1991 are not fully resolved by the supplied text.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal and its experimental realisation with trapped ions defined the first scalable-looking quantum gate architecture, with entangling gates, teleportation, error-correction demonstrations and digital quantum simulation. It has the best coherence times and fidelities of any platform, and is a benchmark for the field.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the 1995 proposal; Blatt's Innsbruck group did much of the experimental advance. Wineland, who shared the 2012 prize, and Monroe, Wineland, Leibfried and Haeffner are not credited here, which weakens the claim of a clean experimental credit. A theory-plus-experiment trio is a plausible structure.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by multiple groups (NIST, Innsbruck, Maryland, Oxford, Quantinuum). Timing is plausible, but the 2012 prize partly covered this area and the 2025 award went to circuit-based macroscopic quantum effects, which adds overlap.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 Wineland prize needs careful framing.
Whether Monroe or Wineland-group experimentalists should be named, which the supplied credit does not allow.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong coupling between a superconducting artificial atom and a microwave resonator experimentally routine, giving the dispersive readout and control for transmon-based quantum processors. It is the basis for the most visible quantum computing hardware, and shows impact beyond physics.
assessment.attribution: Wallraff and Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling in 2004 with the Yale theory of Blais, Girvin and collaborators. Girvin and Schoelkopf are the natural core, with Wallraff for the first demonstration, leaving Blais out, which is an uncomfortable decision. Nakamura, Devoret, Martinis and Clarke also feature in the broader area, including the 2025 prize.
assessment.maturity: Widely replicated and driving industrial development, but the 2025 Nobel prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is close in subject and may make a new prize in this area less timely.
uncertainties: Relation to the 2025 physics prize and to the question of whether circuit QED is distinct enough.
Blais's role in theory is omitted by any three-person configuration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model with tunable parameters, the Mott insulator transition, single-site imaging by quantum gas microscopes and later studies of magnetism and transport. It is a new way to measure many-body physics and is a substantial experimental achievement.
assessment.attribution: Greiner, Bloch and Esslinger are the core experimentalists, with Jaksch, Zoller and Cirac supplying theory but only three names may be proposed, so the experiment-only configuration passes over the theory proposal. The credit allocation between the Mott transition and later microscopy is open.
assessment.maturity: Replicated across many labs and quantum gas microscopes. The ultimate payoff, solving open Hubbard-model questions such as the doped regime, is still not complete, so it is a strong but not fully finished story.
uncertainties: Whether the simulator has answered a problem that classical methods could not.
Credit divided between the theory proposal and several experimental groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Titanium-sapphire gain and passive mode-locking (Kerr-lens and SESAM) created the practical femtosecond laser used in spectroscopy, frequency combs, attosecond science and biomedical imaging. It is an enabling instrument of very wide reach, which I value highly, though the discovery is more a tool than a new physical insight.
assessment.attribution: Moulton demonstrated the Ti:sapphire laser, Sibbett's group Kerr-lens mode-locking and Keller the SESAM. A three-person division is feasible. Others (e.g. Spence, Kapteyn and Murnane, Haus) share credit for the mode-locking mechanism, and the relationship to the 2018 chirped-pulse amplification prize needs framing.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and ubiquitous, so recognition is not premature, with the risk that it could be seen as late or overlapping with existing prizes (Hall and Hansch 2005, Mourou and Strickland 2018).
uncertainties: Whether the committee views this as invention-level work under the physics prize and not a laser-engineering one.
Priority and credit between Kerr-lens and SESAM routes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the Higgs boson required the conception and construction of ATLAS and CMS, instruments of exceptional precision. The discovery completed the Standard Model and is a landmark, though the 2013 prize already recognised the theory.
assessment.attribution: The collaborations include thousands of people, and the 2013 prize did not recognise any experimentalists. Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee are widely seen as the founding spokespersons or conceivers, but the choice among many instrument builders, and the role of the accelerator team and the later spokespersons, is delicate and would need careful argument.
assessment.maturity: The discovery is confirmed by two independent experiments and years of follow-up on couplings. Timely or late rather than premature, but recognition for collaborations conflicts with the three-person limit.
uncertainties: Defining a fair three-person allocation for work done by very large collaborations.
Whether the prize would be seen as a second prize for the same discovery.
